steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our Cieran paper, an AI assistant that helps data analysts rank and create sequential colormaps by learning their preferences from pairwise choices. Explain why colormap design is hard, what is wrong with current options, how Cieran works, our contributions and user study, and the workflow of the tool.

steps.text:
1. Why sequential colormap design is hard
2. Limits of galleries and defaults

4. Cieran: approach
5. Contributions and user study
6. Implementation and workflow

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Colormap design is hard
- analysts decide what colors to use in a chart
- focus: sequential colormaps; orderable, smooth, discriminable colors, perceptual uniformity
- also aesthetic appeal: color-data semantics (cool–warm, positive–negative affects), branding, domain conventions, personal preferences
- perception varies with size/shape of marks, spatial distribution, background color
- interactions -> challenging for typical analyst

2. Galleries/defaults
- small gallery by experts (ColorBrewer) or tool defaults -> limits expressivity
- many other quality examples (e.g. ColourLovers), but rendering vis per colormap + tracking best = time-consuming

3. Manual creation
- suitable colormaps may not exist
- manual: Photoshop; CCC-Tool streamlines for visualization
- most lack technical/design expertise to prototype/refine
- without tools to rank/create -> rely on system default, inadequate presentation

4. Cieran
- pronounced KEE-ruhn; AI assistant; rapidly rank + create sequential colormaps
- training phase: adaptively, iteratively ask to choose between two versions of the visualization, each with a different expert-designed colormap
- color science: alternative choices -> most reliable responses for color preferences; easy task
- update model of aesthetic utility -> rank expert-designed colormaps
- create new colormaps: path planning across CIELAB, learned model as reward signal
- outputs: monotonically decrease in L*, perceptually uniform (Appendix A), cubic B-splines

5. Contributions (§ 5) and study (§ 6)
- active learning strategy -> personalized aesthetic utility model from few inputs
- fast algorithm to create colormaps from utility model
- user study, domain experts (N=12), physical + social sciences, open-ended design task
- suggests/creates pleasing tailored colormaps in around two minutes

6. Implementation
- public Python package, Jupyter Notebooks
- workflow: seed color; fit + process expert colormaps; few (<15) pairs on target vis; rank; create new; selection tool

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
When they visualize data, analysts often have to decide what colors to use in a chart. We focus on designing sequential colormaps, which have to be orderable, look smooth, include discriminable colors, and follow perceptual uniformity. On top of these perceptual guidelines, colormaps should also be aesthetically appealing, and this can depend on color-data semantics (e.g., cool–warm, positive–negative affects), branding, domain conventions, or personal preferences. Also, how we see the colors on a chart changes with the sizes and shapes of the colored marks, their spatial distribution, and the background color of the chart. All these factors and how they interact make colormap design hard for a typical data analyst.

Most of the time people pick a colormap from a small gallery of options designed by experts like ColorBrewer, or from defaults in visualization authoring tools, and this really limits expressivity. There are many other good example colormaps available, for example in communities like ColourLovers, but rendering your visualization with each colormap across galleries and keeping track of the best options can take a lot of time.

Also, a colormap that satisfies the user's needs may not exist yet. People can make new colormaps by hand in tools like Photoshop, and tools like CCC-Tool try to streamline the workflow for visualization. But most people don't have the technical or design expertise with color to prototype and refine colormaps effectively. So without tools that let data analysts efficiently rank existing colormaps or create new ones for their data, people will keep presenting data inadequately by relying on a system default.

4. Cieran
- KEE-ruhn; AI assistant to rank + create sequential colormaps
- training: choose between two versions of the vis, each with an expert-designed colormap; alternative choices -> reliable, easy
- model of aesthetic utility -> rank; new colormaps via path planning in CIELAB, model as reward signal
- outputs decrease in L*, perceptually uniform (Appendix A), cubic B-splines

5. Contributions (§ 5), study (§ 6)
- active learning for personalized utility; fast creation algorithm
- domain experts (N=12), open-ended task; around two minutes

6. Implementation
- Python package, Jupyter Notebooks
- workflow: seed color; fit/process; few (<15) pairs; rank; create; selection tool

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
When they visualize data, analysts often have to decide what colors to use in a chart. We focus on designing sequential colormaps, which have to be orderable, look smooth, include discriminable colors, and follow perceptual uniformity. On top of these perceptual guidelines, colormaps should also be aesthetically appealing, and this can depend on color-data semantics (e.g., cool–warm, positive–negative affects), branding, domain conventions, or personal preferences. Also, how we see the colors on a chart changes with the sizes and shapes of the colored marks, their spatial distribution, and the background color of the chart. All these factors and how they interact make colormap design hard for a typical data analyst.

Most of the time people pick a colormap from a small gallery of options designed by experts like ColorBrewer, or from defaults in visualization authoring tools, and this really limits expressivity. There are many other good example colormaps available, for example in communities like ColourLovers, but rendering your visualization with each colormap across galleries and keeping track of the best options can take a lot of time.

Also, a colormap that satisfies the user's needs may not exist yet. People can make new colormaps by hand in tools like Photoshop, and tools like CCC-Tool try to streamline the workflow for visualization. But most people don't have the technical or design expertise with color to prototype and refine colormaps effectively. So without tools that let data analysts efficiently rank existing colormaps or create new ones for their data, people will keep presenting data inadequately by relying on a system default.

We address this problem with Cieran (pronounced KEE-ruhn), an AI assistant that helps analysts quickly rank and create sequential colormaps when designing communicative visualizations. In its training phase, Cieran adaptively and iteratively asks the analyst to choose between two versions of their visualization, each using a different expert-designed colormap. This builds on prior work in color science which finds that presenting alternative choices gives the most reliable human responses for studying color preferences, and it is also an easy task to respond to. Cieran uses the choice data to update a model of aesthetic utility, and this model can be used to rank expert-designed sequential colormaps. It also creates new colormaps by treating the design as a path planning problem across the CIELAB space, with the learned model as a reward signal. All outputs monotonically decrease in L*, are perceptually uniform (Appendix A), and are interpolated with cubic B-splines, so they meet best colormap design practices.

Contributions. Our main technical contributions (§ 5) are 1. an active learning strategy that induces a personalized model of aesthetic utility for colormaps from few inputs, and 2. a fast algorithm that creates new colormaps given the utility model. We validate the technical approaches with a user study (§ 6) where domain experts (N=12) from physical and social sciences did an open-ended design task. The findings show that Cieran can efficiently suggest and create aesthetically pleasing colormaps tailored to individual users in around two minutes of use.

We implemented the approach as a publicly accessible Python package that is used inside Jupyter Notebooks to rank and create chromatic colormaps according to the aesthetic preferences the user indicates. The workflow of Cieran is:

- • ask the user for a required (seed) component color,

- • fit expert-designed colormaps to this color and process them so they are ordered, smooth, and perceptually uniform,

- • iteratively show a few (<15) pairs of expert-designed colormaps to compare on the user’s target visualization,

- • rank all the expert-designed colormaps from the comparisons,

- • create a new processed colormap matching the user’s aesthetic preferences,

- • show a selection tool so the user can choose their colormap from the ranked choices.

We focus on the design of sequential colormaps, which must be orderable, appear smooth, include discriminable colors, and adhere to perceptual uniformity [1]. Beyond these perceptual guidelines, colormaps should also be aesthetically appealing [2], which can depend on color-data semantics (e.g., cool–warm, positive–negative affects) [3], branding, domain conventions, or personal preferences [4]. Furthermore, how we see colors applied on a chart varies with the sizes and shapes of the colored marks [5], their spatial distribution [6], and the chart’s background color [4]. These factors and their interactions make colormap design challenging for a typical data analyst.

Most often, people choose a colormap from a small gallery of options designed by experts like ColorBrewer [7] or from defaults provided in visualization authoring tools, which greatly limits expressivity. Even though many other quality example colormaps are available, for example in communities like ColourLovers, rendering one’s visualization for each colormap across galleries and tracking the best options can be time-consuming.

Furthermore, pre-existing colormaps that satisfy user needs may not exist. People can build new colormaps manually using tools like Photoshop; tools like CCC-Tool [8] aim to streamline this workflow for visualization. However, most people lack the technical or design expertise in working with color to prototype and refine colormaps effectively. Without tools that let data analysts efficiently rank existing colormaps or create new ones tailored to their data, people will continue to present data inadequately by relying on a system default [9].

We address this issue with Cieran (pronounced KEE-ruhn), an AI assistant that helps analysts rapidly rank and create sequential colormaps when designing communicative visualizations. In its training phase, Cieran adaptively and iteratively asks an analyst to choose between two versions of their visualization, each using a different expert-designed colormap. This approach leverages prior work in color science finding that presenting alternative choices elicits the most reliable human responses for studying color preferences [4] while also being an easy task to respond to [10]. Cieran uses this choice data to update a model of aesthetic utility, which can be used to rank expert-designed sequential colormaps. It also creates new colormaps by treating their design as a path planning problem across the CIELAB space, using the learned model as a reward signal [11].
